title: Repo Time-Lapse Animator
summary: Animate a GitHub repo's file-structure evolution commit-by-commit in the browser, with files appearing, growing, and fading as the codebase changes.
description: A browser tool that fetches a repo's commit history via the GitHub API and renders each commit as a frame: files appear as nodes sized by line count, colored by recency or churn, and edges show directory containment. Scrubbing the timeline plays back the repo's growth as a short animation. Users can export the result as a GIF or MP4 using ffmpeg.wasm. Useful for retrospectives, project demos, and teaching version-control concepts visually.
why_now: ffmpeg.wasm now runs entirely client-side at practical speed, making browser-based video export viable without a backend. GitHub's tree and commit APIs are rate-limit-friendly for small repos.

title: Recurring Feedback Miner
summary: Instructors upload past assignment feedback exports and an LLM clusters recurring patterns into a searchable, reusable comment bank with a drag-and-drop rubric builder.
description: Instructors import Canvas SpeedGrader exports or plain text feedback files. A Flask backend calls Claude to cluster semantically similar comments, label each cluster with a theme (e.g., 'loop boundary errors', 'missing edge-case tests'), and surface representative examples. The React frontend lets instructors browse clusters, promote items to a reusable comment bank, and assemble those comments into a shareable rubric. Over successive semesters the bank grows, surfacing which misconceptions recur year after year.
why_now: Instructors accumulate years of free-text feedback with no tooling to mine it. LLM-based semantic clustering now makes this tractable in a weekend of backend work.

title: Bounded Knowledge NPC Builder
summary: Students build a web adventure where NPCs have explicit knowledge graphs; a constraint checker ensures NPCs never assert facts outside their defined belief set.
description: Students design a small text-adventure world where each NPC has a structured knowledge graph: what it knows, what it believes (with confidence), and what it is explicitly ignorant of. When a player talks to an NPC, the LLM generates dialogue, but a constraint-checking layer inspects every response and flags or blocks statements that exceed the NPC's declared knowledge. Students must define the knowledge representation schema, write the constraint logic, and craft a narrative where the NPC's epistemic limits create meaningful gameplay tension. Reflection prompts connect the design challenge to AI alignment and knowledge-grounded generation.
why_now: Grounded generation and hallucination control are front-of-mind research problems. This assignment makes the challenge concrete and playable, meeting students where game design meets AI safety.

title: NLF-Scaffolded Decomposition Transfer: Does Natural Language Function Specification Build Lasting Problem-Decomposition Skills in CS1?
summary: Investigate whether prompting students to describe functions in natural language before coding durably improves decomposition behavior in later unscaffolded assignments, using Jolly Feedback submission logs as a measurement backbone.
description:
A 2026 SIGCSE study (Becker et al.) found that students using a Natural Language Functions (NLF) tool created roughly 3x more functions and exhibited significantly more decomposition behavior than controls. The scaffolding requires students to articulate function purpose in plain English before writing code, serving as a proxy for the verbal articulation practiced in pair programming. This project asks the follow-on question: does the scaffold produce durable skill transfer, or does decomposition collapse when the scaffold is removed?

Phase 1 (months 1-2) is retrospective: mine existing Jolly Feedback submission logs from CS1 and CS2 C++ courses to establish baseline decomposition metrics (function count, average function length, call-graph depth) per assignment and per student over the semester. Phase 2 (months 3-4) designs a lightweight NLF variant for C++, integrated into the existing Jolly Feedback workflow so students describe each function's purpose before the autograder runs. Phase 3 (months 5-6) deploys the intervention in one CS1 section, compares decomposition metrics on later unscaffolded assignments against a matched control section, and assesses whether early-semester NLF use predicts better late-semester structure. The research connects to Pisan's 'toolchain-first in the copilot era' agenda: if LLM-assisted description teaches decomposition, it may belong in the standard developer workflow from day one.

milestones: Month 1-2: IRB amendment for retrospective log analysis; extract and anonymize Jolly Feedback submission logs; compute baseline decomposition metrics (function count, avg length, call-graph depth) per assignment and student cohort
Month 3: Design NLF prompt integration for Jolly Feedback C++ workflow; pilot with volunteer students outside the study cohort; refine UX
Month 4: IRB approval for prospective classroom study; finalize assignment pairings (NLF-scaffolded early assignments, unscaffolded transfer assignments)
Month 5: Deploy intervention in one CS1 section; collect submission data alongside matched control section
Month 6: Statistical analysis of decomposition transfer (mixed-effects models, student as random effect); write up and submit to SIGCSE or ICER
resources: Claude API for NLF prompt integration
One CS1 section willing to adopt NLF workflow
risks: Retrospective logs may lack consistent metadata across semesters; mitigate by scoping to courses with uniform assignment structure
NLF integration into C++ Jolly Feedback requires moderate engineering effort; scope to a minimal prompt-before-submit UI change
Transfer effect may be confounded by instructor variation; use matched section taught by same instructor or control statistically
